Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one

many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

In ARC-like puzzle solving contexts, requesting demonstrations is a valid strategy to learn the task rule before submitting a solution. The instructions allow for up to 8 demo requests, and each costs 1 point to the scoring metric (though correct submissions do not cost). A wrong submission costs 1 point. A failure to solve (unsolved) costs 16 points.

Given the ambiguity and the high cost of failure, requesting a demonstration pair is the prudent choice to determine the transformation rule (e.g., "replace 1s with 5s", "remove 1s", etc.) accurately. This approach minimizes risk compared to making a blind guess with such a complex-looking input.
